items.title: Edmond Hall Interview, 1957-04-11
items.q: one band I think that I knew that was using a string band, that was Duke Hamilton.

ctx.x: No, I don't remember anybody playing four on the slow blues. I'll tell you another thing, when I went to New York everybody was playing tuba in a regular dance band. You know what we were with stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff

they'd use a string bass. I was surprised to see them, but one band I think that I knew that was using a string band, that was Duke Hamilton. Bro happened to be playing that, and he was playing bass violin, but all the rest of the band was playing tubas.
Did they use banjos much here?

items.title: Edmond Hall Interview, 1958-07-18
items.q: I know a kid right now, and he's working with, uh, with Duke Ellington Man.

ctx.x: Would you advise people that wanted to play just in small groups, like the small New Orleans, or as they call them, Dixieland bands today, would you advise them to learn to read? Or do you think it would be better to not work on them?

Definitely, definitely. Because everything today, of course when we came up with, usually a tune, I could follow a tune if I didn't know that the bass player would know the right chord. Just wasn't listening at the bass note, in fact, they could follow, you know, chord feeding. But today, the way they're writing tunes, you think it's going one way, it's going another, sure. And if you, especially if you're going to make a living, if you're going to make a living for playing these instruments, it's best to learn…
I understand what you're saying. Yeah, he loses the feeling. That sounds, it seems to me here that a lot of these trumpet players do the same thing. Yeah.
